# Genomes {#sec-genomes}

::: {.callout-note title="From the exam description"}
Fundamental differences in how different genomes are constructed. What is
the difference between eukaryotic and prokaryotic genomes?
:::

## Introduction

Genomes differ enormously in size and organisation. Bacterial and
archaeal genomes are typically 0.5–10 Mb, with about one gene per
kilobase. Eukaryotic genomes range from a few megabases in yeasts to more
than 100 Gb in some plants and amphibians. Genome size is not correlated
with organismal complexity (the "C-value paradox"): most of the variation
comes from non-coding DNA, not from gene number. Humans have about 20,000
protein-coding genes, which make up only about 1–2% of a 3.1 Gb genome
[@lander2001; @venter2001; @nurk2022].

**Prokaryotic genomes** are usually a single circular chromosome, often
together with plasmids. They are compact, with short intergenic regions
and genes that lack introns. Functionally related genes are often
organised in operons that are transcribed as one mRNA. Gene content is
very dynamic. Genes are frequently gained by horizontal gene transfer and
lost again, so strains of the same species can differ in a large part of
their gene repertoire. This led to the concept of the *pan-genome*: a
core shared by all strains plus a large accessory set
[@tettelin2005; @koonin2008; @treangen2011]. The first complete genome of
a free-living organism, *Haemophilus influenzae*, was sequenced in 1995
[@fleischmann1995].

**Eukaryotic genomes** are divided between several linear chromosomes
with centromeres and telomeres, packaged into chromatin inside the
nucleus. Genes are split into exons and introns, and alternative splicing
lets one gene produce several protein isoforms. Most eukaryotic DNA is
intergenic or intronic. A large part of it consists of transposable
elements and other repeats, for example about half of the human genome.
Regulatory elements such as promoters, enhancers and insulators can lie
far from the genes they control. Chromatin folds into loops and
topologically associating domains that bring these elements together
[@liebermanaiden2009]. How much of the non-coding genome is "functional"
is still debated. The ENCODE project found biochemical activity across
most of the genome [@encode2012], but critics argue that activity does
not imply function. Eukaryotes also carry organelle genomes in
mitochondria and chloroplasts, which are remnants of bacterial
endosymbionts.

Why are genomes so different? One influential explanation is
population-genetic. In organisms with large effective population sizes,
such as most prokaryotes, selection is efficient enough to remove even
slightly costly DNA. In organisms with small populations, such as
multicellular eukaryotes, drift allows introns, mobile elements and
duplicated genes to accumulate [@lynch2003]. Comparisons across genomes
suggest that there are statistical regularities in genome evolution, for
example in the distributions of family sizes and evolutionary rates
[@koonin2011].

## Key concepts

- Genome size, gene number and gene density across bacteria, archaea and eukaryotes; the C-value paradox
- Prokaryotic genome organisation: circular chromosomes, operons, plasmids, compact genomes, GC skew
- Eukaryotic genome organisation: introns and splicing, alternative splicing, large intergenic regions, centromeres/telomeres
- Repeats and transposable elements; segmental duplications
- Non-coding RNAs and regulatory elements; what fraction is "functional" (ENCODE debate)
- Organelle genomes and endosymbiosis
- Pan-genomes: core vs. accessory genes; horizontal gene transfer
- 3D genome organisation: chromatin, TADs (Hi-C)
- Population-genetic explanations of genome complexity (Lynch)

## Key papers

### Reviews — start here

- @koonin2008 — genomics of bacteria and archaea: the emerging dynamic view of the prokaryotic world.
- @lynch2003 — the origins of genome complexity.
- @koonin2011 — are there laws of genome evolution?

### Landmark genomes

- @fleischmann1995 — the first complete genome of a free-living organism (*Haemophilus influenzae*).
- @lander2001 — the public human genome draft.
- @venter2001 — the Celera human genome.
- @nurk2022 — the complete human genome.

### Genome function and organisation

- @encode2012 — ENCODE: an integrated encyclopedia of DNA elements.
- @liebermanaiden2009 — Hi-C: the 3D organisation of the human genome.
- @tettelin2005 — the microbial pan-genome.
- @treangen2011 — horizontal gene transfer in prokaryotes.
